messages.author: 9ac59323a4312d0d
messages.subject: methylkit question
parts:
Hello,

My name is Claire and I am a current graduate student at the University of Washington.  I am comparing 6 samples using whole-genome bisulfite sequencing using the R package methylKit and have a few questions I'm hoping to get answered. 

First, I am wondering if I can compare these samples without designating a single sample as a control.  And if this isn't possible how this is going to skew my results by assigning a sample to be a control when in reality it isn't?  I am comparing DNA methylation patterns throughout various developmental stages so I therefore do not have a control sample in my dataset.  

Also, I am wondering how exactly the differentially methylated regions (DMRs) are calculated.  I am assuming that the coverage is taken into account for the calculation of DMRs, and am a bit confused by my results.  Specifically, I am only obtaining 15 DMRs between two samples (out of ~112,000 loci), however my correlation coefficient is only 0.82 between these two samples.  Any input you can give me would be greatly appreciated and I thank you for your time.
--
Claire E. Olson

University of Washington
School of Aquatic and Fishery Sciences

students.washington.edu/che625

messages.author: 38c56d0e82a34280
messages.subject: Re: [methylkit_discussion] methylkit question
parts:
Just to clarify- are you doing an n-of-1 study, with the data drawn at different time points? If so, I would suggest you run the analysis multiple times, with a different time point as the 'case' (treatment=1) each time (you can use the reorganize fuction in methylKit to change your treatment vector to do this). This will allow you to identify methylation differences that are characteristic for each time point. See how that compares to similar array-based studies as appropriate for your tissue and species: see this paper and some of its references. 

Two different tests are used depending on the number of samples: if you're comparing 1 vs 1, Fisher's exact test is used. Otherwise, logistic regression (also known as a binomial GLM with a logit link) is used to compare the means of the two groups. In either case, coverage is taken into account. If you're using the get.methylDiff function, it's filtering for sites with qvalues<.01 and methylation differences of >25%. Depending on your data, this may be too stringent- you have a relatively low number of sites, so I'd consider raising the qvalue threshold.

Dhruva

messages.author: ab8277113f65c05e
messages.subject: Re: [methylkit_discussion] methylkit question
parts:
differential methylation by definition requires a control group. If you are interested in comparing two stages of development it is OK to assume one of them is the control just remember which one is which when you do the interpretation.

 But, I guess what you are interested is specific methylation patterns that change over the course of the development (more than 2 timepoints ?). You can do multiple things to make headway on this. In addition, in methylKit, DMRs are the regions of the genome that are predefined, such as equi-width tiles over the genome, or promoter regions. So I assume that you tiled your data since you want to get DMRs (regions).

You can read-in all your samples at once keeping the order of the developmental stages, do the tiling and then do unite(). then get the methylation matrix using percMethylation() then do clustering on the rows of the matrix as Dhruva suggested and make a heatmap. But this will take a lot of time if you are using whole-genome data. Alternative is to use PCA on the matrix of methylation values. This could get you some patterns that explain the variation of your data, and those patterns may correspond to actual changes in methylation that are shared by multiple DMRs.

Another alternative is to calculate the variation of the rows of the methylation matrix, and get the ones that have high variation and do clustering or PCA on them to see the shared patterns among regions of varying methylation.


Here is discussion about coverage in differential methylation calculation
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/methylkit_discussion/Li$20/methylkit_discussion/_6LlMiPH_98/xZVsXbl-sMgJ
